$comment: Independent verification of every bibliographic and substantive assertion in vice-and-reason.reference-brief.md. Nothing here was taken on the brief's authority. Where verification and brief disagree, verification wins.

methods.bibliographic: Live Crossref (api.crossref.org) DOI resolution, polite pool. Items with thin Crossref coverage were cross-checked against OpenAlex (api.openalex.org). Truncated DOIs in the brief were re-resolved by bibliographic search, never reconstructed by guessing digits.
methods.substantive: Direct text extraction from the fixture PDF (unpdf/pdf.js, the project's own ingestion parser) followed by literal string search. A substantive claim counts as verified only when the paper's own wording supports it.
methods.notVerified: Characterizations of third-party works that were reachable only as metadata/abstract are explicitly marked 'metadata_only' and must NOT be promoted to accepted facts downstream.

bibliographic.brief: 'The Nature of Immorality,' Social Philosophy and Policy (originally 1990; Cambridge online record later)
bibliographic.source: crossref + the fixture PDF's own note 2
bibliographic.actual: Two distinct publications with identical pagination: (a) the journal article — Social Philosophy and Policy 7(1), 22-44, 1989, DOI 10.1017/S026505250000100X; and (b) the book chapter Irwin himself cites — in E. F. Paul, D. Miller and J. Paul (eds.), Foundations of Moral and Political Philosophy, Oxford: Blackwell, 1990, pp. 22-44.
bibliographic.evidence: Irwin's note 2 reads: 'A vigorous statement of some of these objections to Aristotle is presented by Jean Hampton, "The Nature of Immorality," in E.F. Paul, D. Miller and J. Paul (eds.), Foundations of Moral and Political Philosophy (Oxford: Blackwell, 1990), pp. 22-44, at pp. 29-31.'
bibliographic.resolution: The brief conflated the two. The journal version is 1989, not 1990; the 1990 date belongs to the Blackwell volume. Irwin cites the book, and pins the relevant objection to pp. 29-31 specifically.
bibliographic.downstreamRequirement: A run that surfaces this source must not assert 'Social Philosophy and Policy, 1990'.

substantive.claim: Irwin states the puzzle in the article's abstract: vicious people must be guided by reason since they act on decision (prohairesis), yet cannot be guided by reason since they are said not to live in accordance with it.
substantive.anchor: ABSTRACT. Aristotle's account of vice presents a puzzle: (1) Vicious people must be guided by reason, since they act on decision (prohairesis)

substantive.claim: Irwin says the puzzle is resolved by examining the pursuit of the fine and the expedient, the connexion between vice and pleasure, and the particular kind of regret of the vicious person.
substantive.anchor: once we examine Aristotle's account of (a) the pursuit of the fine and of the expedient; (b) the connexion between vice and the pursuit of pleasure; (c) the particular kind of regret

substantive.claim: Irwin concedes he develops Aristotle beyond Aristotle's explicit remarks.
substantive.anchor: I have developed some of his remarks beyond anything he says
substantive.note: The brief says this concession comes 'near the middle of the paper'. It occurs at the head of section 8 of 11 — accurate.

substantive.claim: Irwin closes by conceding the account fits some vices better than others, working less well for greed, vindictiveness, and domination.
substantive.anchor: Cowardice, intemperance, and sloth might plausibly be understood as following one's inclinations and failing to raise some evaluative questions about them. But it is more difficult to accept this analysis for greed, or vindictiveness, or the desire for power and domination.
substantive.discrepancy: The brief lists the well-fitting vices as 'cowardice and intemperance'. Irwin's own list is three: cowardice, intemperance, AND SLOTH. A run that reproduces only the brief's two is reproducing the brief's omission, not the paper.
substantive.downstreamRequirement: The generated edition must name all three.

substantive.claim: Irwin adapts part of his exposition from Aquinas, specifically the distinction among sin from passion, ignorance, and deliberate badness, in note 1.
substantive.anchor: Aquinas sees that to understand sin, we must distinguish its different sources. The three that he discusses are passion, ignorance, and deliberate badness (certa malitia).
substantive.note: Confirms both the content and the brief's claim about its placement in note 1. 'certa malitia' is the Latin term Irwin uses and should surface in the glossary module.

substantive.claim: Irwin invokes Callicles and Thrasymachus as figures who appear to choose vice on principle, then denies Aristotle treats ordinary vicious agents that way.
substantive.anchor: This might seem to be the outlook of Callicles and Thrasymachus, as Plato presents them. In that case, virtuous and vicious people agree in deciding on actions because they are fine; they simply differ about which actions these are.

substantive.claim: Callicles in the Gorgias illustrates the vice of intemperance specifically.
substantive.anchor: Callicles in the Gorgias illustrates this feature of vice, and specifically of intemperance.

substantive.claim: Irwin cites Jean Hampton as a forceful statement of the objection that Aristotle's account of vice is unstable.
substantive.anchor: A vigorous statement of some of these objections to Aristotle is presented by Jean Hampton
substantive.seeAlso: hampton-immorality — the brief's citation details for this work are wrong; the attribution itself is right.

substantive.claim: Irwin names Annas as a carefully defended statement of the inconsistency charge, and Broadie as criticizing her.
substantive.anchor: A more carefully defended statement of the view that Aristotle is inconsistent appears in Julia Annas... Her argument is criticized by Sarah Broadie, Ethics with Aristotle (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991), p. 177n41.
substantive.correction: The brief calls Broadie 'the [most sympathetic] predecessor Irwin cites, especially on self-love and friendship.' Irwin's actual note cites Broadie narrowly, as the critic of Annas at a single footnote (p. 177n41). The brief overstates the role. Treat Broadie as a cited critic of the inconsistency charge, not as a broad precursor.

substantive.claim: The paper draws on Nicomachean Ethics I, II, III, VII, and IX rather than treating Book VII and Book IX as unrelated.
substantive.evidence: Irwin's note 3 chains EN citations across 1166b, 1168a, 1169a, and 1110b in a single note; term frequencies across the paper show sustained engagement with decision (41), the fine (35), incontinence (30), regret (25), and self-love (11).

substantive.claim: Vice is distinguished from incontinence because the vicious act on decision.
substantive.evidence: Stated in the abstract and developed across sections 5 ('Types of Decision') and 8; 'incontinen*' occurs 30 times.

substantive.claim: The virtuous person's orientation is to the fine, the vicious person's to the expedient.
substantive.evidence: Sections 6 ('Pursuing the Fine') and 7 ('Pursuing the Expedient without the Fine') are dedicated to exactly this contrast.

influenceDisciplineNote: Verification found NO case where the brief inferred influence from mere similarity — it consistently hedged to 'parallel, related, or part of the same debate'. That discipline is expected of the generated edition too: Elliott 2016 naming Irwin is explicit engagement and may be labelled as such; Nielsen, Barney, Marechal and Moss inhabiting the same problem-space is 'parallel/same-debate' and must NOT be labelled influence.
